CLOSURE OF HAL AND BEGUMPET AIRPORTS - SOME LEGAL AND PROCEDURAL ISSUES
28. During the visit of the Committee, there were wide ranging discussions with various
stakeholders of the Airports in Bengaluru and Hyderabad. The representatives of the Airports
Authority Employees Union gave a detailed presentation before the Committee inter alia on the legal
and procedural issues involved in the closure of HAL Airport at Bengaluru and Begumpet Airport
at Hyderabad.
29. During the discussion at Bangaluru, the representatives of the Airports Authority Employees
Union (AAEU) submitted before the Committee that the Government was adopting a strange policy
of privatising and closing down the profit-making airports of Airports Authority of India; AAI was
struggling to manage to cross-subsidise non-profit making airports in the remote areas, from the
revenue it was earning through the profit-making airports. The Committee was informed that during
2004, Prime Minister of India had formed a Tripartite Committee to look into various issues
connected with airport infrastructure. The Chairman of the Tripartite Committee had given
categorical assurance to the Joint Forum and to AAEU on 13.10.06 that even after the opening of
BIAL Airport, HAL Airport will be functioning and airlines will be given the freedom to choose
between the two airports.
30. AAEU have also brought before the Committee various facts and arguments in connection
with the closure of HAL Airport, Bengaluru. Various points raised by Airports Authority of India
Employees Union were forwarded by the Committee to the Ministry of Civil Aviation on 3rd
October, 2008 for their comments. Even after reminders the Ministry did not offer their comments
till the writing of this Report.
31. Some of the major issues submitted before the Committee by them during the deliberations
are given are in the following paragraphs:
31.1 No comprehensive Privatisation Policy for the airports
31.1.1 It was argued that in the post-liberalisation era, privatisation had been done in sectors in
which only public sector organisations were present like Airlines, Insurance, Banking, Petroleum
etc.: In all these above sectors, not even a branch of any PSUs were closed down after private
players entered and a healthy competition was allowed between them resulting in quality services
at much competitive price. Also, the total volume of business in all these sectors also increased
due to competition. The Government, however, has signed an agreement with BIAL to close down
HAL Airport owned by AAI for commercial operations. This action of GoI is not at all consistent
with its own policy in other sectors.
31.2 Violation of 150 Km. norm
31.2.1 The Committee was informed that in 1997, Government of India announced a policy on
airport infrastructure which said that no Greenfield airport will normally be allowed within an aerial
distance of 150 kilometers of an existing airport. Where it is allowed as a second airport in the
same city or close vicinity, the parameters for distribution of traffic between the two airports will
be clearly spelt out. But the Bengaluru and Hyderabad Greenfield airports were permitted within 150
kms of radius of the existing airports in violation of the said policy. Also, the distribution of the
traffic between the two airports was also not spelt out.
31.2.2 It was further contended that as per this “a Greenfield airport may be permitted where an
existing airport is unable to meet the projected requirements of traffic or a new focal point of
traffic emerges with sufficient viability. It can be allowed both as a replacement for an existing
airport or for simultaneous operation. This aspect will have to be clearly spelt out in the notice

9
inviting tenders.” Therefore, this fact ought to have been clearly spelt out in the notice inviting
tender in the case of Bengaluru and Hyderabad. But the notice inviting tender did not contain any
clause about closure of HAL Airport.
31.3 Airports Authority Act, 1994
31.3.1 It was further contended that there was no provision in the AAI Act 1994, to close down
an AAI airport, particularly, ‘only for commercial purposes’. The representatives of AAEU further
submitted that an MoU signed between AAI and Karnataka Industrial and Infrastructure
Development Corporation (KSIIDC) in 199.9 for developing the Greenfield Airport also did not have
any clause on closing down of HAL Airport for commercial operations, after the proposed
Greenfield airport was opened. Shareholders’ Agreement, 2002  also did not mention about this.
Hence the closing of HAL Airport is in violation of the very MoU which has envisaged the
Greenfield Airport project near Bengaluru.
31.3.2 The Committee was informed that many viability enhancement methods provided in the
procedure guideline to set up Greenfield Airports have been suggested including giving land on
concessional price, exempting taxes etc. But these methods do not envisage closure of existing
airport as a method to enhance the economical viability of a Greenfield airport project.
31.3.3 The Committee notes that the closure of HAL Airport was not mentioned in the
tender for Bengaluru Greenfield Airport. Naturally, all the parties who participated in the
tender process would have made their offers on this basis only. Making an offer of Closure
of HAL Airport, after the Notice Inviting Tender (NIT), appears to be a clear violation of
the due process.
31.3.4 As regards the restriction on having another airport within 150 Kms of existing
airport, granting permission to start a new Greenfield airport within that radium prima facie
seems to be in violation of the Government policy on airport infrastructure.
31.3.5 The pronounced policy also states that if an airport was allowed within an aerial
distance of 150 kms of an existing airport, a passenger sharing formula has to be evolved.
In the present case, the Government not only allowed the new airports to come up within
a distance of 150 kms but also closed down the existing profit-making airports, not to speak
of passenger sharing formula.
31.3.6 The Committee notes some merit in these arguments made by the representatives
of AAEU. It also feels that the closure of old airports at Bengaluru and Hyderabad appears
to have been done in haste. It is no doubt deprives the AAI a good amount of revenue that
it needs to cross-subsidize airports in remote areas.
31.4 Concession Agreement - Irregularities
31.4.1 V arious arguments questioning the validity of the Concession Agreement signed between the
private companies and the Government were made before the Committee. For example, the
Concession Agreement (CA) dated 5th July, 2004 has a clause making it obligatory on GoI to
publish a notification declaring that HAL Airport will not be available for commercial civil aviation
from the date of opening of the new BIAL Airport at Devanahalli, Bengaluru.
31.4.2 The representatives of AAEU claimed that the Concession Agreement which was initially
prepared and approved by the Cabinet did not provide for the closure of HAL Airport. However,
allegedly, the clause related to HAL Airport closure was brought at a later stage into the
Concessional Agreement, after a demand made to this effect by the BIAL.

10
31.4.3 The Committee’s attention was drawn to a Notification issued by Government of India on
the 16th May, 2008 for HAL Airport which inter alia stated that in exercise of powers conferred
by Section 5A of the Aircraft Act, 1934, read with Rules 11 and 78 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937
and in deference of the contractual commitments including Clause 5.5 of the Concession Agreement
signed between Government of India and BIAL on the 5th July, 2004 and consequent on
commissioning of the Bengaluru International Airport at Devanahalli, w.e.f. 0001 hours of
23rd May, 2008, the HAL Airport at Bengaluru will no longer be available for “commercial civil
aviation operations”.
31.4.5 The representatives of AAEU pointed out that the powers under Section 5A are limited to
the matters mentioned in Section 5 and can be used only in two situations (a) if the security of
India is in danger and (b) if the safety of the Aircraft is in danger. In the given case of HAL
Airport, both these reasons are not present. Moreover, GoI itself says in the Notification that it has
used these powers “in deference of the contractual commitments including Clause 5.5 of the
Concession Agreement”, which clearly shows that the use of the powers u/s 5A was not due to
the above said reason but only in deference to the reasons best know to the Ministry and perhaps
to BIAL also.
31.4.6 They further argued that though the Notification says about closing HAL Airport for
“Commercial civil aviation operations” such a phrase is not defined in any of the Acts or rules
applicable in India (Aircraft Act 1934, Aircraft Rules 1937, Civil Aviation Requirements (CAR)).
31.5 Impossibility of the implementation of the Notification
31.5.1 With regard to the above notification, the representatives of AAl submitted that its
implementation is not possible. They stated that at HAL Airport Air Traffic Control (ATC) controls
almost half of the Bengaluru airspace even after the commissioning of BIAL. HAL ATC is an integral
part of Bengaluru HAL Airport. Even for the operations of BIAL Airport, HAL ATC operations are
necessary. HAL A TC still controls and will continue to control all aircraft operations including
commercial operations through the part of Bengaluru airspace controlled by it. Hence, it is a myth
that by this notification, commercial civil aviation operations of HAL Airport has been banned.
31.5.2 Even after the notification HAL Airport is being used by all types of Chartered Aircrafts.
Both parties to the Notification have already violated the notification by express action. BIAL has
violated the notification by giving permission to air taxi operations of M/s Deccan Aviation Limited
and Global Vectra Helicorp from and to HAL Airport. GoI has also violated when it has informed
Deccan Aviation that they do not have any objection for air taxi operations out of HAL Airport as
BIAL has no objection.
31.5.3 The Committee notes that commercial civil aviation activities are continuing in the
Bengaluru HAL Airport with the consent of the management of BIAL and Government of
India, whereas the Concession Agreement and the notification issued by the Government of
India clearly prohibits any commercial aviation activity. This shows that if the Government
wants, they can operationalise the old airports notwithstanding the Concession Agreement.
The Committee is of the considered view that HAL Airport at Bengaluru and Begumpet
Airport at Hyderabad may be made operational for domestic civil aviation.
31.5.4 The Committee notes that the Government has taken shelter of Section 5A of
Aircraft Act 1934 to close down HAL airport. However, Section 5A talks of closing of any
airport when there is danger to the aircraft/country. The above reason is totally irrelevant
for the instant case. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should
revisit various provision of the Concession Agreement to ensure that all the illegalities, etc.
are removed from it that are creating all kind of misgivings in the people’s mind.

11
31.6 NOC for setting up of Bengaluru Greenfield Airport by Ministry of Defence
31.6.1 It was contended before the Committee that as per the Aircraft Rules, 1937 and CAR, NOC
by the Ministry of Defence is mandatory for setting up of an airport. Ministry of Defence has
given its NOC for Devanahalli Greenfield Airport vide its letter No. 3(48)/02/D (Air. II) dated
03.03.04. But this NOC was subject to a condition that the operations at HAL Airport, Bengaluru
will continue even after the BIAL becomes functional and the choice of airport to be utilized should
be left to the operators/commuters/general public.
31.6.2 On the same ground, the license given to BIAL for airport operations by DGCA as per the
Aircraft Rules, 1937 (Rule 78) also becomes subject to this conditional NOC given by Ministry of
Defence. In view of this, they argued, GoI Notification for closing of HAL airport as well as
Aerodrome License of BIAL issued by DGCA ipso facto became null and void.
31.6.3 The Committee notes that the NOC for setting up of Bengaluru Greenfield Airport
by Ministry of Defence made it amply clear that the operations at HAL Airport Bengaluru
will continue even after the BIAL becomes functional and the choice of airport to be utilized
should be left to the operators/commuters/general public. Same is true about the license
issued to BIAL by the Director-General, Civil Aviation. In terms of Notification dated the
16th May, 2008, the HAL Airport stands closed for commercial operations. However, it is
still being used for chartered flights, air taxi services and VIP flights. The Committee fails
to understand that in such a situation, how the losses being incurred by the HAL Airport
would be compensated as desired by the Ministry of Defence while issuing NOC for the new
airport at Bengaluru.
31.7 Licensing of Airports
31.7.1 As per the Aircraft Rules 1937 (Rule 78) and also Civil Aviation Requirements (CAR)
aerodromes can be licensed either for public use that will be available to all persons on equal terms
and conditions or for Private Use  by the licensee and by individuals specifically authorized by the
licensee. It may be noted that private use of aerodromes exclude the operation of schedule flights
therefrom.
31.7.2 Their argument was that as per the above provisions of relevant rules and CAR, an
Aerodrome can be either for public use or private use only. There cannot be a third category, “for
public use but not for commercial civil aviation operations” as has been exactly done by the
notification about closer of the HAL Airport. It is thus clear that an aerodrome which is for public
use should be available to all persons on equal terms and conditions. Hence, an aerodrome like HAL
Airport, which is available for public use cannot be, closed for commercial civil aviation operations
and no such restriction can be imposed on an Airport for public use it was contended.
31.7.3 The Committee would like to have Ministry’s response on this point.
31.8 Similar International Examples
31.8.1 The Committee has learnt that Don Mueang International Airport (Old Bangkok Airport) was
closed completely on opening of new Suvarnabhumi Airport on 28.09.06, which was 40 kms away
from the city. However, mainly due to demands of low cost carriers and the higher costs at the new
Airport, old airport was reopened on 24.03.2007, without restrictions on distance or aircraft capacity.
31.8.2 Another example brought to the notice of the Committee was Dallas Love Field Airport
(USA) that was closed after new DFW International Airport become operational. There was no
Concession Agreement between the Operator and the Regulator or the Federal Government.
However, Southwest Airlines was permitted to operate from the old Airport even after opening of
DFW International Airport, as it was not a signatory to this Agreement.

12
31.8.3 The Committee takes note of these examples of more than one airport co-existing
in the cities to cater to the needs of various types of passenger requirements. The
Committee feels that the same can be applied in case of Bengaluru and Hyderabad Airports
also and the old airports in these cities may be made functional.
31.9 Role of AAI
31.9.1 It was further argued that AAI was an authority created by an Act of Parliament (55 of
1994) with no budgetary support and it was continuously making profit since inception and has
a Mini-ratna Status. The Airports Authority of India operates 127 airports including 16 international
airports, 83 domestic and 28 civil enclaves at defence airfields. AAI thus control and manages the
entire Indian airspace of 2.8 million square nautical miles. AAI provide communication navigation
and surveillance (CNS-ATM) services at all the airports in the country, including Greenfield
Airports. AAl’s competency in airport infrastructure is well known. AAI has constructed many
airports and has consulting projects in other countries like South Yemen, Libya, Algeria, Nauru,
Seychelles and Afghanistan.
31.10 Impact on AAI
31.10.1 The Committee was informed that due to the closure of HAL Airport alone, the estimated
revenue loss to AAI was around Rs 389 crores in 2007-08. Similarly, due to the closure of
Begumpet airport, Airports Authority of India lost and estimated revenue of Rs.221.15 crore during
this period. Thus, it lost of Rs.610 crore in the year 2007-08.
31.10.2 In addition to the above losses, AAI was losing revenue on account of RNFC (Route
Navigational Facility Charges) in other AAI Airports by cancellation of outbound flights from BIAL
Airport to other AAI Airports all over the country. It was underlined that AAI was running airports
in non-profit remote areas of the country as National obligations.
31.10.3 The Committee notes most  of the reasons advanced for the opening of the HAL
Airport at Bengaluru are applicable to  the Begumpet airport in Hyderabad also.
31.10.4 The committee notes that the equity contribution of the consortium of private
companies in BIAL is only Rs. 240/- crores. The rest of the financing has come from state
support, AAI, Government of Karnataka and by way of debt from financial institutions. The
land was also given on a concessional rate. The same is the case with HIAL also. The equity
contribution of the private companies is around Rs. 330/-  crores. The rest of the finance has
come from Government agencies and by way of debt from financial institutions. The
Committee notes that with the kind of resources and expertise that the Airports Authority
of India has, these airports could have been easily developed and operated by the Airports
Authority of India itself.
31.10.5 The Committee is, therefore, of the view that being leading airport infrastructure
provider, the Airports Authority of India which has got the resources and expertise should
have a better say in the modernization of airports in the country. The Committee
recommends that any future Greenfield airports or Brownfield airports project must be done
under the management of Airport Authority of India. JVCs can be formulated but the
Airports Authority of India must have a majority holding in the company and management
control must rest with it.

“The Committee while appreciating the steps taken by the State Governments of

recommends that the Ministry pursue this long standing issue with other State

Governments so that uniformity of tax on ATF can be maintained. Since the cost of

recommends that Ministry of Finance should sympathetically consider and give

57. The Committee notes that one of the basic purposes of handing over the
modernization task of Mumbai and Delhi airports to the Joint Venture Company was to
complete it within the given time limit. However, the Committee feels that JVC has not
been able to meet the time frame as mentioned in the agreement to complete various
modernization projects (mandatory projects) and such projects are running behind schedule.
The Committee recommends the Government to institutionalize the monitoring mechanism
to avoid delays and cost over runs in the execution of the projects at Mumbai and Delhi
airports.
58. The Committee notes that the airlines and passengers are the main sources of
revenues for airport developers at Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Mumbai and Delhi and with rising
fares and cost cutting across the sector, developers are pruning infrastructure plan and
opting for ways to cut cost and install low priced facilities. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the developers in these airports should be restrained from charging user
development fee and the Government should not agree to it. The airport operators may be
directed to implement the modernization plan as per the agreements within the scheduled
time limit instead of concentrating on revenue earning from commercial activities.
59. The Committee while visiting the Mumbai and Delhi airports had noticed the poor
state of affairs at the airports as a problem leading to crowded terminal, sitting space was
inadequate, passengers were left searching for trolleys, food articles were sold over and
above the MRP, lack of basic amenities/canteen facilities, higher charges towards security,
lounge rental, aviation services, parking, telephone and other facilities, no residential space
for the ATC staff, no co-ordination with the user agencies and airport operators, no round
the clock help service available; delay in execution of building projects at Mumbai and
Delhi, inadequate inter-terminal passenger transportation facilities and airlines were not
finding space for parking bays in the airport terminal and charges for this were very high.
60. The Committee observes that due to lack of adequate civic utilities like toilets,
drinking water fountains etc. outside arrival/departure hall of all the four airport,
passengers/tourists experienced difficulties. There was also lack of toilet facility at car/taxi
parking area outside the airports. The Committee observes that Airport Operators should
not ignore the needs of such people. The Committee recommends that toilet and drinking
water facilities should be provided outside the arrival/departure lounge and parking areas
in order to avoid inconvenience to the passengers and co-passengers.
61. Some instances of impolite behavior with the passengers at the airports was brought
to the notice of the Committee. This type of behavior does not go well with the tourists and
creates an unpleasant atmosphere. The Committee desires that officials deputed at the
airport, should strictly be asked to be courteous and polite with the passengers particularly,
the tourist from other countries. The officials deputed at the airport and dealing with the
passengers/tourists should be more careful, polite, helpful and tourist friendly.
62. The Committee recommends that a coordination mechanism may be evolved for
regular interaction among various stakeholders of Chattrapati Shivaji International Airport
with representation from agencies such as MIAL, Airports Authority of India, Employees
Unions of Airports Authority of India, various airlines etc. This mechanism will iron out
differences among the stakeholders of the airport and will enable smooth functioning of the
airport.
63. The Committee, after visiting the airports at Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru and
Hyderabad and after considering the facts and information made available to it in respect
of modernization and development of private airports as well as closure of HAL and

21
Begumpet airports, has gained impression that had all the processes and procedures been
done in far more transparent and acceptable manner, most of the objections and
controversies could have been avoided. Right from arranging finances for participating joint
venture companies, giving thousands acres of land on concessional rates and allowing them
to use the land commercially, signing OMDA and Concession Agreements favorable to JVCs
and closure of existing airports, etc. are some of the areas about which there are lot of
misgivings in the minds of people and media keeps writing about these.
64. Besides, the Airports Authority of India, advertently or inadvertently, appears to not
being given its due. Even though, ATC operations of all the airports are still with them, the
closure of HAL and Begumpet airports and placing Airports Authority of India virtually at
the mercy of the management of private airports, speaks a lot about it. The manner in
which the Concession Agreement and OMDA wer e signed has also invited wide criticism and
these are alleged to have violated the existing policies, guidelines, norms, rules, etc. The
Committee feels that there appears to be some truth in the apprehensions that are being
raised against the Government in the entire exercise of privatizing the airports, developing
the Greenfield airports and the related matters. The Committee expects that the
Government of the day to provide convincing explanation to all the points, raised in this
report to clear the apprehensions that are being flown thick and wide. It is for the
Government to clarify the entire matter.

OBSERV ATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS — AT A GLANCE
BENGALURU INTERNATIONAL AIRPOR T LIMITED (BIAL) AND HYDERABAD
INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT LIMITED (HIAL)
The Committee found the plan and design of the Greenfield airports to be of the
international standard with certain useful facilities for the comfort and convenience of the
passengers, for example, adequate and efficient check-in counters, self check-in machines
and quick immigration clearance, large number of shops, eateries, etc. However, the
Committee also came across certain areas that needed immediate attention. For example,
the Committee found, that the passengers at the Greenfield airports have to pay
exorbitant prices for food items. The eateries are charging much more than the MRP,
which is against the Supreme Court order. There is no separate canteen for the
employees and the staff working at the airports. The drivers and others who are waiting
outside the airports have no affordable canteen facility and basic amenities like toilets
and bathrooms. The Committee recommends that the Government should ensure that the
Greenfield Airports at Bengaluru and Hyderabad provide basic facilities to the drivers and
passengers and stop the eateries from charging exorbitant prices. Private airlines have to
cough up hefty amounts for parking bays and aerobridges, security charges, lounge
rentals, telephone rentals and other facilities at the new airports. (Para 13)
The parking charges for vehicles are also quite heavy at the new airports. At
Bengaluru, it is Rs.40/- per hour and Rs.20/-per additional hours. The Committee is
surprised to know that at Hyderabad airport, a vehicle while entering the airport for
dropping or picking up a passenger has to pay Rs.35/- per trip. The Committee notes that
space earmarked for passenger seating areas was inadequate and numbers of seats are
also not adequate, causing inconvenience to the passengers during peak times. This is so
because much of the airport space has been let out for commercial use and given to
shopping outlets and F&B outlets. There is conspicuous absence of lounges at these
airports. There is a need for creation of additional reserved lounge for VIPs and
passengers. To help and guide the passengers at these airports, there should be round-the-
clock help service at these airports. There were inadequate facilities provided for free
drinking water at these airports. More drinking water fountains should be installed. The
emergency medical facilities for treatment of the passengers in case of sudden illness
should be in place in all the new airports as has been done at the new Hyderabad airport.
(Para 14)
The Committee recommends that the flight delay or cancellation must be reported
to passengers well in time to avoid hardships to the passengers. The baggage handling
process should be strengthened so as to reduce the baggage delivery time and hardship
to the passengers. Apron driving discipline should be maintained to avoid any accident on
apron and staff should be given proper training for the driving skills and behaviors. There
should be integration of air and ground surveillance information along with flight related
data to enhance air travel safety and efficient air traffic management. (Para 15)
The private operators should recognize various staff welfare Committees of Airports
Authority of India and others working at these airports. There should be regular
consultative and coordination meeting of all the stakeholders at the new airports so as to
resolve the different issues/grievances. (Para 16)
22

23
The Committee learnt that it was discouraging for the short-haul passengers to
take air travel after the new airports. A higher User Development Fee (UDF) was being
charged by the new airport developers from the passengers. The user development fee
added with high taxi/bus fares due to long distances, compel the passengers to use other
means of transport such as road and, trains for the short distance destinations. This has,
in fact rendered the air travel from these airports added with high ATF prices, just
prohibitive. (Para 17)
The Committee notes that the Task Force on Financing Plan for airports (July,
2006) had recommended that the users should not be burdened with ADF/UDF for
financing at the airport projects. This is particularly important in the context of the policy
objective to make civil aviation a mass, rather than an elitist model of travel and to
make air travel more affordable. After taking into account various aspects and the above
recommendation of the Task Force the Committee feels that the imposition of UDF on
passengers is a retrograde step contravening the Task Force recommendations and
recommends that the UDF imposed on passengers may be withdrawn immediately and no
more UDF may be imposed on passengers in any of the airports. (Para 18)
CAPACITY OF BIAL AIRPORT
The Committee notes that the Government of India appears to be unconcerned
about the obligation of BIAL to construct and provide an airport as per the concession
agreement. Even the area and capacity were not verified before permitting to open new
and closing HAL Airport. This appears to be an irregularity committed by Government of
India in this matter. (Para 19.6)
The Committee notes that hundreds of crores of rupees were spent for developing
infrastructure at the old airports at Bengaluru and Hyderabad but it is lying unutilized
due to the closure of airports for commercial purposes. Another interesting thing brought
to the notice of the Committee is that the old airports, the HAL Airport and Begumpet
Airport, are being used for operation of VIP flights, Non-schedule Flights, General
Aviation, Helicopter-Taxis, etc. During the deliberations of the Committee the Airports
Authority of India reported that there is absolutely no problem in opening up two airports
simultaneously in a city. The Committee therefore, recommends that the old airports of
Hyderabad and Bengaluru may be used exclusively for short haul flights which are
operating from the nearby airports. (Para 24)
The Committee also notes that the closure of HAL airport led to loss of jobs due
to reduction of flights and due to closure of airlines operators. Thousands of direct and
indirect workers also lost their jobs, this also includes trolley retrievers, small time
vendors, taxi drivers, auto drivers, loaders etc. Despite the assurances given by the BIAL
and HIAL managements, they have not been accommodated in the new airports. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that all those people who are directly or indirectly
affected due to closure of the HAL Airport and Begumpet Airport may be given preference
and suitably accommodated at the new Green Field Airports. (Para 25)
The Committee is of the opinion that the HAL Airport is most convenient for
common public due to it being situated closer to the City Centre, easy accessibility and
availability of multi-mode transport options like Bus, Auto, Taxis, even 2-wheeler, etc.
HAL Airport, therefore, would be more convenient and economical for public compared to
BIAL due to absence of UDF and less transportation cost due to multiple modes and
shorter distance. Less time in coming and going from the airport is also important aspect
in this regard. (Para 26)

24
The Committee further recommends that the old airports may be made operational
for short-haul passengers. Moreover, this is the practice being followed in many of the
major cities in the world wherein more than one airport exists. There is no reason or
justification for keeping the hundreds of crores of worth infrastructure at the old airports
idle just to be used for VIP and other flights. (Para 27)
CLOSURE OF HAL AND BEGUMPET AIRPORTS—SOME LEGAL AND PROCEDURAL ISSUES
The Committee notes that the closure of HAL Airport was not mentioned in the
tender for Bengaluru Greenfield Airport. Naturally, all the parties who participated in the
tender process would have made their offers on this basis only. Making an offer of
Closure of HAL Airport, after the Notice Inviting Tender (NIT), appears to be a clear
violation of the due process. (Para 31.3.3)
As regards the restriction on having another airport within 150 kms of existing
airport, granting permission to start a new Greenfield airport within that radium prima
facie  seems to be in violation of the Government policy on airport infrastructure.
(Para 31.3.4)
The pronounced policy also states that if an airport was allowed within an aerial
distance of 150 kms of an existing airport, a passenger sharing formula has to be evolved.
In the present case, the Government not only allowed the new airports to come up within
a distance of 150 kms but also closed down the existing profit-making airports, not to
speak of passenger sharing formula. (Para 31.3.5)
The Committee notes some merit in these arguments made by the representatives
of AAEU. It also feels that the closure of old airports at Bengaluru and Hyderabad
appears to have been done in haste. It is no doubt deprives the AAI a good amount of
revenue that it needs to cross-subsidize airports in remote areas. (Para 31.3.6)
CONCESSION AGREEMENT – IRREGULARITIES
IMPOSSIBILITY OF THE IMPLEMENTATION OF THE NOTIFICATION
The Committee notes that commercial civil aviation activities are continuing in the
Bengaluru HAL Airport with the consent of the management of BIAL and Government of
India, whereas the Concession Agreement and the notification issued by the Government
of India clearly prohibits any commercial aviation activity. This shows that if the
Government wants, they can operationalise the old airports notwithstanding the
Concession Agreement. The Committee is of the considered view that HAL Airport at
Bengaluru and Begumpet Airport at Hyderabad may be made operational for domestic civil
aviation. (Para 31.5.3)
The Committee notes that the Government has taken shelter of Section 5A of
Aircraft Act 1934 to close down HAL airport. However, Section 5A talks of closing of any
airport when there is danger to the aircraft/country. The above reason is totally irrelevant
for the instant case. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should
revisit various provision of the Concession Agreement to ensure that all the illegalities,
etc. are removed from it that are creating all kind of misgivings in the people’s mind.
(Para 31.5.4)
NOC FOR SETTING UP OF BENGALURU GREENFIELD AIRPORT BY MINISTRY OF DEFENCE
The Committee notes that the NOC for setting up of Bengaluru Greenfield Airport

25
by Ministry of Defence made it amply clear that the operations at HAL Airport Bengaluru
will continue even after the BIAL becomes functional and the choice of airport to be
utilized should be left to the operators/commuters/general public. Same is true about the
license issued to BIAL by the Director-General, Civil Aviation. In terms of Notification
dated the 16th May, 2008, the HAL Airport stands closed for commercial operations.
However, it is still being used for chartered flights, air taxi services and VIP flights. The
Committee fails to understand that in such a situation, how the losses being incurred by
the HAL Airport would be compensated as desired by the Ministry of Defence while
issuing NOC for the new airport at Bengaluru. (Para 31.6.3)
The Committee takes note of these examples of more than one airport co-existing
in the cities to cater to the needs of various types of passenger requirements. The
Committee feels that the same can be applied in case of Bengaluru and Hyderabad
Airports also and the old airports in these cities may be made functional. (Para 31.8.3)
ROLE OF AAI
IMPACT ON AAI
The Committee notes most of the reasons advanced for the opening of the HAL
Airport at Bengaluru are applicable to the Begumpet Airport in Hyderabad also. (Para 31.10.3)
The Committee notes that the equity contribution of the consortium of private
companies in BIAL is only Rs.240/- crores. The rest of the financing has come from State
support, AAI, Government of Karnataka and by way of debt from financial institutions.
The land was also given on a concessional rate. The same is the case with HIAL also. The
equity contribution of the private companies is around Rs. 330/- crores. The rest of the
finance has come from Government agencies and by way of debt from financial
institutions. The Committee notes that with the kind of resources and expertise that the
Airports Authority of India has, these airports could have been easily developed and
operated by the Airports Authority of India itself. (Para 31.10.4)
The Committee is, therefore, of the view that being leading airport infrastructure
provider, the Airports Authority of India which has got the resources and expertise should
have a better say in the modernization of airports in the country. The Committee
recommends that any future Greenfield airports or Brownfield airports project must be
done under the management of Airport Authority of India. JVCs can be formulated but
the Airport Authority of India must have a majority holding in the company and
management control must rest with it. (Para 31.10.5)
MODERNIZATION OF MUMBAI AND DELHI AIRPORTS
Master Plan
The above problems brought before the Committee needs serious attention of the
Government. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should suitably
intervene to ensure that the burden is not passed on the passengers. It should furnish
its response to these points for the Committee’s consideration. (Para 40)
The Government should take adequate and essential steps to equip the airports
which are 30 to 40 minutes flying time from the major airports to meet any exigencies.
The Committee is of the view that this problem can be solved if the Government
expedites development/modernization of non-metro airports. (Para 42)

UNIFORM TAXATION OF ATF
This issue has now become more relevant in the context of current crisis faced by
airlines that is largely attributed to high cost of ATF. It is sad that airlines are resorting
to retrenchment of their staff. The Committee hopes that Government would take
adequate steps to see that civil aviation sector is not affected and young trained
manpower do not get desperate. With regard to the problem of high price of ATF, the
Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation in its 138 report which inter-alia  stated
that –
‘‘The Committee while appreciating the steps taken by the State Governments of
Kerala and Andhra Pradesh in reducing the Sales Tax on ATF from 32% to 4%
recommends that the Ministry pursue this long standing issue with other State
Governments so that uniformity of tax on ATF can be maintained. Since the cost
of fuel is an important component of cost structure, reduction in taxes on ATF will
definitely have a positive impact on the airfares. The Committee once again
recommends that Ministry of Finance should sympathetically consider and give
approval to the proposal of Ministry of Civil Aviation regarding notifying ATF as
‘Declared Good’ under Section 14 of Central Sales Tax Act on priority basis to all
the aircrafts so that sales tax on ATF could be contained within the maximum rate
of 4 per cent. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry of Finance
may also discuss the issue with the State Governments and try to persuade them
to reduce the sales tax on ATF. The Committee is of the opinion that the success
of the concept of low cost carrier mainly depends on the taxation of ATF which is
very much on the higher side. The Committee feels that reduction in airfares will
bring more new passengers to the airports.’’ (Para 43)
The Committee recommends that the women employees should not be relocated to

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture, having been authorised by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby
present this One Hundred and Forty-third Report on “Action Taken by the Government on the
Recommendation/Observations of the Committee contained in its One Hundred and Thirty-fourth
Report on Demands for Grants 2008-09 of the Department of Shipping”.
2. The One Hundred and Thirty-fourth Report of the Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture was presented to the Parliament on the
17th April, 2008.
3. The Action Taken Replies on the recommendations of the Committee contained on its
One Hundred and Thirty-fourth Report were received from the Department of Shipping on the 23rd
October, 2008.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on the
18th December, 2008.
SITARAM YECHURY
N
EW D ELHI; Chairman,
December 18, 2008 Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Agrahayana 27, 1930  (Saka) Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture.

1
REPORT
This Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the
observations/recommendations as contained in its One Hundred Thirty-fourth Report on Demands
for Grants (2008-09) of the Department of Shipping, which was presented to the Parliament on
17th April, 2008.
2. Action Taken Replies have been received from the Government on 23rd October, 2008 in
respect of all the observations/recommendations contained in the Report. These have been
categorized as follows:—
(i) Recommendations/observations that have been accepted by the Government:
Para Nos. 10, 11, 28, 48, 55, 63, 64, 70, 81, 82 and 97 Total: 11
(ii) Recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view
of the Government replies:
Para Nos. 39 and 101 Total: 2
(iii) R ecommendations/observations in respect of which replies of the Government have not been
accepted by the Committee:
Para Nos. 100 Total :1
(iv) Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Government are still
awaited:
Para Nos. 16, 20, 23, 24, 31, 35, 40, 51, 58, 69, 75, 93 and 94 Total :13
3. The Committee desires that final replies in respect of the recommendations, which
have been categorized as interim replies by the Committee should be furnished to it at the
earliest.
4. On scrutiny of the said Action Taken Replies, the Committee has made observations on each
item of the action taken/proposed to be taken by the Department of Shipping. The
recommendations of the Committee contained in the One Hundred Thirty-fourth Report, action
taken thereon by the Government and recommendations/observations of the Committee on each
item of action taken have been given in the succeeding paragraphs.
ANALYSIS OF ANNUAL PLAN 2008-09
(Recommendation at Para 10 and 11))
5. The Committee observes that the Department has projected a requirement of Rs.68971.48
crore for the entire Eleventh Plan. Against this requirement, the Planning Commission approved an
allocation of Rs. 67173.40 crore to the Department for carrying out major activities i.e.
development of Major Ports, Inland Water Transport, procurement of Dredgers and connected
activities for the Dredging Corporation of India, constructions of landing facility in Andaman and
Nicobar Islands, post Tsunami rehabilitation works, Ship Buidling, Rail connectivity for the ports
and Sethusamudram Ship Channel Project etc.
6. The Committee strongly deplores the tendency of Planning Commission and the Ministry of
Finance for imposing cuts on the amount demanded by the Department as per their pressing needs.

2
The Committee feels that if the Department of Shipping has to attain the national growth of 9%
in the Eleventh Plan period, it will require huge and well planned funding. Thus, the Government
spending for the Department of Shipping will have to be significantly stepped up from the present
level to meet the growth targets. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the
Department should be provided with Rs.68971.48 crore by the Planning Commission and the
Ministry of Finance for the Eleventh Plan period as their original proposal and ensure that no
projects/scheme proposed by the Department would languish for want of funds. The Committee
also recommends the Department to take appropriate caution and remedial action to absorb in time
the allocation made to them.
Reply of the Government
7. The recommendations of the Committee have been brought to the notice of Planning
Commission as well as Ministry of Finance for compliance.
Further recommendation/observation of the Committee
8. The Committee notes that as per the recommendations of the Committee, the
Department of Shipping has requested the Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance for
providing Rs.68971.48 crore as per original proposal for the entire Eleventh  Plan. The
Committee feels that if the Department has to achieve the growth targets then the Planning
Commission and Ministry of Finance should consider to allocate the projected outlay.
PORT SECTOR
(Recommendation at Paras 16 and 20)
9. The Committee is perturbed to note that the Department of Shipping has projected higher
plan outlays of Rs.4271.27 crore during the year 2007-08 which was drastically reduced to
Rs.3075.34 crore at RE stage and ultimately, the Department failed to utilize the reduced amount
too. The Department utilized Rs.2517.00 crore during 2007-08 against the budget estimates of
Rs.4271.27 crore and surrendered an amount of Rs.1754.27 crore as compared to the BE for the
year. The Committee observes that the saving affects almost all the major activities of Department
of Shipping be it Inland Water Transport, Shipping, Ports, Lighthouses and Lightships, Shipbuilding
etc. and the actual expenditure incurred has always been abysmally low compared to the estimated
amount. The Committee is not satisfied with the reasons furnished by the Department for non-
utilization of the allocations for their being either vague or of routine in nature. The Committee does
not approve the practice being followed by the Department which has been asking for higher
allocations year after year, but the implementation of projects and schemes were poor as ground
realities were not taken into account while formulating and implementing the projects. The
Committee is pained to note that although they have repeatedly recommended for formulation of
realistic plans and schemes but no action have been taken by the Government on those
recommendations. The Committee expects that intensified monitoring mechanism which is being put
in place by the Department, would ensure that budgeted amounts earmarked at the BE stage are
fully utilized during 2008-09. At the same time, The Committee recommends that a meaningful and
relevant programmes and policies be formulated for regular infusion of funds in various projects
and schemes in all quarters of the financial year for total utilization of plan outlays and if required,
the Government should review all the on-going schemes periodically for re-allocation of the
budgeted amount. The Committee would like to be apprised of the action taken by the Government
in this regard.
10. The Committee is distressed to note that there has been under-utilization of plan allocation
in the port sector and finds that in BE 2007-08, an outlay of Rs.2109.76 crore consisting of GBS

3
of Rs.498.49 crore and IEBR of Rs.1611.27 crore was provided to the port sector as against this
allocation, the anticipated expenditure is Rs.1694.71 crore comprising of Rs.359.62 crore GBS and
Rs.1335.09 crore IEBR. In the Annual Plan 2008-09, again higher budgetary allocations to
Rs.3650.97 crore has been made in anticipation of modernization of port sector though the actual
expenditure has always remain low as compared to budget estimates. The Committee feels that
since ports have a crucial role to play in facilitating the India’s total EXIM trade, the Department
should devise the concrete and concerted efforts for achieving the desired targets. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that projections of required fund should be made more realistic so that
resources are not unnecessarily kept unutilized and are allocated more judiciously and projects are
monitored scrupulously to achieve the envisaged targets. The Committee would also like to be
apprised of the achievement of the physical and financial targets in the port sector during the
current financial year.
Reply of the Government
11. The above recommendations of the Committee have been forwarded to all the Major Ports
and other concerned Organizations for compliance.
Further recommendation/observation of the Committee
12. The Committee notes the reply and desires to have the expenditure pattern of the
Department of Shipping for the year 2007-08 and 2008-09 up to December, 2008 to ascertain
the progress of fiscal management, utilization of budgetary allocation and the details of the
physical and financial target set for achieving the progress. The Committee recommends
that for better physical and financial monitoring of the projects, the Department should
strengthen its own monitoring mechanism in a well coordinated manner at apex level to
achieve optimum utilization of funds.
(Recommendation at Para 23 and 24)
13. The Committee notes that the Department has delegated the financial powers to the port
trusts under the instructions issued by the Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance for
timely execution, formulation, appraisal and approval of the projects to be funded through the
public investment and also for public private partnership projects. The respective jurisdiction with
respect to Standing Finance Committee (SFC), Departmental Expenditure Finance Committee
(Departmental EFC), Main Expenditure Finance Committee (Main EFC), Committee of Secretaries
(CoS), Public Investment Board (PIB) or Public Private Partnership Appraisal Committee (PPPAC)
is determined on the basis of the total cost of the project/schemes for the entire plan period. The
Committee notes with dismay that the spreparation and clearance of SFC/EFC/CCEA/PPPAC
proposals require undue long time and in some cases it takes precious long time of about 2-3
years. The Committee see no justification in such a situation wherein many schemes/plans/projects
of the Department has an outlay for a period of 5 years mentioned on paper only but actually
cannot be utilized till the approval of the SFC/EFC/CCEA/PPPAC remains pending. The Committee
urges the Department as well as the concerned Appraisal Agencies to seriously introspect over
the delays which are so detrimental for the progressive functioning of the Shipping and Port
Sectors.
14. The Committee also desires that steps should be taken well in time by the Department/
Planning Commission/Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) to avoid any such
recurrences for the future and a limited stipulated time frame should be fixed for clearance from
the Planning Commission and SFC/EFC/CCEA/PPPAC approval.

4
Reply to the Government
15. The recommendations of the Committee have been brought to the notice of Planning
Commission as well as Ministry of Finance for compliance.
Further recommendation/observation of the Committee
16. The Committee notes that the Department of Shipping has taken up the matter with
the Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance for removal of procedural hurdles in the
preparation and clearance of project proposals. The Committee does not see any difficulty in
the Government establishing a single high powered agency for quick clearance of projects
proposals for the Shipping and Port Sectors with a view to address the procedural hurdles and
administrative delays. The Committee therefore, recommends the Department to pursue the
matter with the Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance for setting up of the single
high powered Committee for the progressive functioning of the Shipping and Port Sector.
CAPACITY UPGRADATION IN MAJOR PORTS
(Recommendation at Para 28)
17. The Committee takes note of the efforts being made by the Department of Shipping in
implementing schemes for augmenting the cargo handling capacity and productivity of all major
ports under National Maritime Development Programme (NMDP) to meet India’s EXIM trade
requirements. The Committee also notes that during 2007-08, the aggregate capacity of major ports
was 504.75 mt pa which was a little over the total traffic of 469.37 mt. up to February, 2008.
The Committee feels that the projected increase in the traffic also requires increase in capacity in
ports. During Eleventh Plan period, the ports require a projected capacity addition of 1016.55 mt pa
to meet the overall projected traffic of 1008.95 mt. of which the share of major ports will be
708.09 mt. The Committee also observes that the bulk of capacity augmentation projects at major
ports will be undertaken through Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs) and captive users. The
Committee recommends the Department of Shipping to devise plans for holistic and integrated
development of major ports and make efforts to encourage the private sector investments including
FDI for creation and maintenance of port infrastructure including cargo handling capacity at major
ports. The Committee also recommends the Department to provide enabling policies, regulatory
framework and institutional monitoring mechanism support to raise port efficiency, productivity,
equipment and performance level in order to face global challenges of merchandize trade.
Reply of the Government
18. Noted for compliance.
Further recommendation/observation of the Committee
19. The Committee notes that as per its recommendation the Department has taken
steps for augmenting capacity building schemes at major Ports for the Eleventh Plan. The
Committee recommends the Department to remove the bottlenecks and provide facilitative
and legislative support to encourage the private sector investments for major capacity
upgradation infrastructure projects at all major Ports.
CONTAINERIZATION IN MAJOR PORTS
(Recommendation at Para 31)
20. The Committee notes that containerization of traffic is growing steadily and significantly

5
with dedicated capacity for handling containerized cargo in major ports. The Committee, however,
is constrained to note that the major ports did not significantly contribute to merchandise global
trade making thereby India’s export costlier and imports less competitive. The Committee observes
that a high powered committee has been constituted by the Government to report on the matter
of creation of infrastructure facilities for handling containers at major ports, identification of
problems of congestion and explore areas of improvement in logistics chain and to suggest
measures to increase India’s share in world maritime trade as in India only two regional hub ports
are operational at Jawaharlal Nehru and Chennai Ports for maximizing direct to destination cargo.
The report of high powered committee is awaited. The Committee recommends the Department of
Shipping to ensure that there is no laxity in its efforts pending report of the high powered
Committee for development of more hub ports in the country for transshipment of containerized
cargo for growth of overseas maritime merchandise trade.
Reply of the Government
21. Noted. The Department of Shipping is planning to construct a number of container
terminals on BOT basis through Public Private Partnership (PPP) mode at various Major Ports.
Some of the container terminals which are expected to be awarded in the next two years are as
shown below:
(i) Container Terminal at Ennore — Estimated cost Rs.1300 crore.
(ii) Mega Container Terminal at Chennai — Estimated cost Rs.3105 crore.
(iii) Container Terminal at Tuticorin — Estimated cost Rs.150 crore
(iv) Container T erminal at Kolkata — Estimated cost Rs.1233 crore
(v) Development of Container Terminal north of NSICT, Jawaharlal Nehru Port–Estimated
cost Rs. 600 crore
(vi) Fourth C ontainer Terminal at Jawaharlal Nehru Port–Estimated cost Rs.4100 crore.
22. In addition License Agreements have been signed for (i) International Container
Transshipment Terminal at Cochin Port which is expected to be operational by November, 2009
(ii) Development of 2nd Container Terminal at Chennai Port which is expected to be operational
by 2009-10 and (iii) Construction of two offshore container terminals at Mumbai Port which is
expected to be operational by 2010-11.
Further recommendation/observation of the Committee
23. The Committee notes the reply.
PORT CONNECTIVITY
(Recommendation at Para 35)
24. The Committee is perturbed to note that port efficiency is still continuing to be impeded
mainly because of slow evacuation of cargo from ports. It also notes with dismay that various rail-
road connectivity projects in the ports of Haldia, Paradip,Chennai, Ennore, Tuticorin, Cochin, New
Mangalore, Mormugaon, Jawaharlal Nehru Ports are either lagging behind schedule or not
sanctioned for implementation. The Committee feels that the slow progress of projects not only
undermines the competitiveness of Indian Ports but also vitiates the environment of investment in
the country. The Committee recommends the Department to augment the rail-road connectivity of

6
major ports with the hinterland for smooth flow of present as well as future traffic. The Committee
also recommends the Department to fix some realistic and achievable targets and put in place
institutional monitoring and review mechanism so that projects could be completed in a time bound
manner and in case of delay, the responsibility must be fixed.

ESTABLISHMENT OF REGULATORY AUTHORITY
(Recommendation at Para 39)
27. The Committee notes that the Department of Shipping is in the process of formulating a
Maritime Policy for the maritime sector which seeks to ensure a coordinated development of Ports,
Shipping, Inland Water Transport, Ship Building and Ship repairing with the objective to upgrade and
modernize the port infrastructure in India to benchmark its performance against global standards. The
Committee also gathered from the replies that the regulatory authority will be setup at an appropriate
time. The Committee observes that since much of the activities in the port sector are taking place
with private participation, there is need to establish regulatory authority well in time and that too
before coming across any problem for better control, co-ordination and monitoring for achieving
excellence in the port and shipping sector besides addressing serious security implications. The
Committee, therefore, recommends the Department of Shipping to take steps for setting up of a
regulatory authority on the pattern of Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) and Insurance
Regulatory and Development Authority (IRDA) for creating a level playing field
and foster healthy competition and to encourage investments for the shipping and port sector besides
monitoring performance standards and adjudication of disputes and disposal of appeal thereof.
Reply of the Government
28. Noted. In so far as the Major Ports are concerned, there is an autonomous body, namely,

TAMP fixes the Scale of Rates (SoR) for various services rendered by the Major Ports. The
Department of Shipping has recently issued guidelines to TAMP for upfront fixation of tariffs for
projects which are to be taken up through private sector participation through the Public Private
Partnership (PPP) mode. Thus, the TAMP is regulating the various activities at the Major Ports
through tariff fixation.
Further recommendation/observation of the Committee
29. The Committee notes that the Tariff Authority for Major Ports (TAMP) is regulating
the various activities at the Major Ports only. The Committee however has recommended
to set a regulatory authority to regulate the shipping and port sector and not for major
ports only and wish to have the opinion of the Government in this regard.
(Recommendation at Para 40)
30. The Committee also recommends the Department to formulate maritime policy for the private
sector participation for improving quality, efficiency and increasing competition for coordinated
development of Ports, Shipping, Inland Water Transport, Ship building and Ship repairing.
Reply of the Government
31. Noted. The Department of Shipping is in the process of formulating the Maritime Policy in
consultation with the concerned Ministries and Planning Commission. The changes/modifications
suggested by various Ministries/Departments have been incorporated and action is being taken to
finalize the policy.
Further recommendation/observation of the Committee
32. The Committee notes the reply.

CALCUTTA DOCK LABOUR BOARD
(Recommendation at Para 48)
33. The Committee strongly criticize the lackadaisical approach of the Government in releasing the
one time grant of Rs.738.71 crore for financial assistance on account of payment of (arrears of
pension and pensionary dues of Calcutta Dock Labour Board (CDLB) and setting up of a corpus fund
for discharging pension and pensionary liabilities of the employees. The Committee notes with anguish
that even after repeated recommendations of the Committee, the Government has not approved any
specific proposal to mitigate the sufferings of these poor pensioners. The Committee observes that
a scheme for merger of CDLB with Kolkata Port Trust (KoPT) and financial restructuring of KoPT
is under consideration of the Committee of Secretaries (CoS). The Committee unanimously opines
that unless the Government is actually willing and come forward to support the employees and
pensioners of CDLB, they will continue to die in harness under the resource crunch. The Committee,
therefore, strongly urges the Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance to consider favourably the
legitimate and long-felt needs of the pensioners and provide much needed one time grants immediately
in order to settle the arrears of pension and pensionary dues of the employees of Calcutta Dock
Labour Board, who have rendered their services to the nation.
Reply of the Government

pensioners, workers and employees of Calcutta Dock Labour Board in the following manner:

Waterway Authority of India (IWAI) or Kolkata Port Trust (KoPT) or Shipping Corporation
of India (SCI), so that the infrastructure and expertise of CIWTC can be utilized for
development of waterways transport.”
Reply of the Government
87. It is submitted that the Cabinet has decided in favour of disinvestment of CIWTC minus
RBD. Action has already been initiated in compliance of the said decision. The Corporation has been
making losses continuously since operation in the longer stretches of national waterways as of now
are not commercially viable compelling the Government to go for its disinvestment. The
disinvestment of CIWTC is not likely to affect the role/activities of CIWTC. It will only result in
charge of share holding pattern and in the nomenclature of the Corporation. The Inland Water
Transport activities too are not likely to be affected by the disinvestment of the Corporation.
Further, since Cabinet has already decided in favour of disinvestment of CIWTC (minus RBD), no
feasibility study for merger of CIWTC with other organizations was conducted. The issue of
physical amalgamation of CIWTC (minus RBD) with various organizations such as IWAI, KoPT or
SCI was raised in various communications received from Hon’ble Members of Parliament and other
dignitaries and was examined in the Ministry and not found feasible.

21
88. The corporation has about 100 IWT vessels out of which 40 are operational. While some
of the non-operational vessels are awaiting repair some are beyond economic repair. CIWTC
operated 47 voyages in NW-1 between 2004 and 2006 at the behest of IWAI. The route is,
however, non-economical.
Further recommendation/observation of the Committee
89. T he Committee is perturbed to note that despite being recommended by the
Committee a number of times the Government has not taken setps to improve the financial
health of the CIWTC. The Committee does not agree with the Government that with the
disinvestment of CIWTC, the role and activities of CIWTC will not be affected. The
Committee, therefore, strongly recommends the Department to conduct a feasibility study
for merger of CIWTC with other organizations such as IWAI, KoPT or SCI for the holistic
development of inland water transport.
DEVELOPMENT OF WATER TRANSPORT IN ANDAMAN AND NICOBAR AND
LAKSHADWEEP ISLANDS
(Recommendation at Para 101)
90. The Shipping Corporation of India with its two owned passenger-cum-cargo vessels and 27
managed vessels operates domestic passenger-cum-transportation services between mainland and
Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep group of islands on behalf of the Government of
India. Presently, Andaman and Nicobar Islands administration has 22 vessels comprising of 18
passenger vessels and 4 passenger-cum-cargo vessels, Union Territory of Lakshadweep has 5
vessels comprising 1 passenger-cum-cargo vessel, 3 passenger vessels and one bunker barge. The
Committee observes that water transport is the life-line of these groups of islands for their
interconnection with the mainland and within islands. The Committee notes that this sector has
been neglected for so many years without any fund infusion for modernization of the vessels and
purchase of additional vessels. Due to this, the populations of these islands are suffering to a great
extent. The Committee further notes that in the Demand for Grants for the year 2008-09 no
financial allocation has been made for improving the interconnectivity and water transport in
Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep islands. The Committee, therefore, recommends
to the Government of India to take immediate steps for improving inter-islands connectivity of the
islands of Andaman and Nicobar and Lakshadweep for mitigating the problems of connectivity
between these islands. The Committee also recommends that sufficient Budgetary Allocation may
be provided for augmenting the water transport connectivity in these islands.

OBSERV ATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS — AT A GLANCE
ANALYSIS OF ANNU AL PLAN 2008-09
The Committee notes that as per the recommendations of the Committee, the
Department of Shipping has requested the Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance
for providing Rs.68971.48 crore as per original proposal for the entire Eleventh Plan. The
Committee feels that if the Department has to achieve the growth targets then the
Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance should consider to allocate the projected
outlay. (Para 8)
PORT SECTOR
The Committee notes the reply and desires to have the expenditure pattern of the
Department of Shipping for the year 2007-08 and 2008-09 upto December, 2008 to
ascertain the progress of fiscal management, utilization of budgetary allocation and the
details of the physical and financial target set for achieving the progress. The Committee
recommends that for better physical and financial monitoring of the projects, the
Department should strengthen its own monitoring mechanism in a well coordinated
manner at apex level to achieve optimum utilization of funds. (Para 12)
The Committee notes that the Department of Shipping has taken up the matter
with the Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance for removal of procedural hurdles
in the preparation and clearance of project proposals. The Committee does not see any
difficulty in the Government establishing a single high powered agency for quick clearance
of projects proposals for the Shipping and Port Sectors with a view to address the
procedural hurdles and administrative delays. The Committee therefore, recommends the
Department to pursue the matter with the Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance
for setting up of the single high powered Committee for the progressive functioning of
the Shipping and Port Sector. (Para 16)
CAPACITY UPGRADATION IN MAJOR PORTS
The Committee notes that as per its recommendation the Department has taken
steps for augmenting capacity building schemes at major Ports for the Eleventh Plan. The
Committee recommends the Department to remove the bottlenecks and provide facilitative
and legislative support to encourage the private sector investments for major capacity
upgradation infrastructure projects at all major Ports. (Para 19)
The Committee notes the reply.
(Para 23)
PORT CONNECTIVITY
The Committee is perturbed to note the slow progress of most of the various
ongoing/sanctioned railway-road connectivity projects at the major Ports. It also
constrained to note that the connectivity projects in the Ports of Paradip, Tuticorin,
Kandla, Kolkata, Mormugao, Haldia, Mumbai, Ennore and Cochin are either lagging
25

26
behind schedule or the work was not awarded for implementation. The Committee
recommends the Department to pursue the matter with the Ministry of Railways and the
Department of Road Transport and Highways for timely completion of the various projects.
(Para 26)
ESTABLISHMENT OF REGULATORY AUTHORITY
The Committee notes that the Tariff Authority for Major Ports (TAMP) is
regulating the various activities at the Major Ports only. The Committee however has
recommended to set a regulatory authority to regulate the shipping and port sector and
not for major ports only and wish to have the opinion of the Government in this regard.
(Para 29)

(Para 32)

the unpaid arrears to pensioners, workers and employees of Calcutta Dock Labour Board
on the recommendations of the Committee of Secretaries. However, the Committee
recommends the Department to release payments of pension and pensionary dues to the
employees of the CDLB at the earliest. The Committee of Secretaries should also be
pursued to review its decision and allow financial assistance to KoPT in the form of grants
instead of loans. (Para 36)
TONNAGE TAX REGIME
The Committee notes the reply.

Cruise Shipping Policy for tile growth of cruise shipping in the country. The Committee
hopes that with the implementation of the Policy, a sustained and structured growth for
the sector could be achieved. (Para 42)

The Committee notes that a group was constituted to go into the problems of
multiplicity of taxes being faced by the shipping industry and its report has been
submitted to the Government. The Committee also notes that based upon the
recommendation of the report, the Department is consistently making efforts for
extension of fiscal incentives to Indian Shipping Industry which are adversely impacting
the growth of the shipping sector with the Ministry of Finance. The Committee
recommends the Department to vigorously follow up the matter for rationalization of
taxes ailing the shipping sector with the Ministry of Finance at the apex level.
(Para 45)

enhancement in intake and augmenting existing training facilities to ensure quality in

endeavour to address the continuing shortage of maritime human resources by setting up
new institutes in this field. (Para 49)

Restructuring of Hindustan Shipyard Limited, Visakhapatnam has been circulated to

comments at the earliest for placing before the Cabinet for a final decision. (Para 56)

Hindustan Shipyard Limited to the Ministry of Defence the interest of the employees of
HSL and the pending dues of the retired employees will be taken care of. (Para 59)

The Committee notes that a final cabinet note for granting Rehabilitation-cum-
Restructuring package of Hooghly Dock and Port Engineers Limited has been sent for
consideration and approval of Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA). The
Committee recommends the Department to follow-up the matter for grant of
Rehabilitation-cum-Restructuring Package to HDPEL so that the financial health of the
Company could be sustained. (Para 62)
INLAND WATER TRANSPORT
The Committee notes the measure adopted by the Department for the growth of
IWT sector in the country. It also notes that a taskforce has been functioning in the
Department to review the progress of IWT projects on quarterly basis. The Committee
recommends the Department to remove the procedural bottlenecks which causes the delay
in approval and execution of the projects so that the physical and financial targets could
be achieved in a big way. (Para 66)
The Committee notes that the Department of Shipping has prepared an Action Plan
to make the existing three National Waterways fully functional by providing a threshhold
level of required infrastructure namely fairway, terminals and navigational aid and these
are at various stages of implementation. The Committee, however, once again
recommends the Department to provide institutional framework and basic infrastructural
facility for accelerated development of Inland Water Transport sector in the country.
(Para 72)
The Committee notes the reply.
(Para 75)
The Committee notes with dismay that the infrastructure required to make the
total transport cost competitive from origin to destination using IWT mode is yet to be

loading/unloading and aids for 24 hrs. navigation. It however, notes that the utilization of
the National Waterways for transportation of cargo is expected to increase significantly

28
after completion of the implementation of Action Plan and demonstration vessel runs. The

Committee recommends the Department to provide adequate investment, policy framework

study report. (Para 80)
The Committee notes the reply that the Department has not experienced any

11. The Committee notes that the growth of Motor V ehicles in India is unprecedented. The
process of liberalization and globalization augmented the number of vehicles to beyond the
imagination of our planners of road sector development. The infrastructure available is not at all
commensurate with the growth of vehicles. The Committee also notes that the allocation to the
Department is almost static in real terms. There is an increase of 20% in Annual Plan outlay and
7.6% in budgetary support. The above increase in Annual Plan outlay and budgetary support may
not be adequate even to meet the increase in cost. Thus, it poses a great mismatch between the
availability of the road infrastructure and vehicular population.
12. Inadequate development of road sector will result in congested roads, traffic jams, recurring
accidents and chaos in the road sector. Moreover, the development of road infrastructure is
immensely important to sustain the growth of the economy. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Government should allot funds to the Department of Road Transport and
Highways so as to ensure the development of road infrastructure in proportion to the growth of
vehicles. The Committee further recommends that demands of the Department may be acceded to
at the RE stage.

under Phase-IV but the project has not been approved till date by the Government. The Committee
recommends that NHDP Phase-IV may be considered by the Government for approval immediately.

timely implementation.

16. NHDP Phase-II comprising of 4 laning of 6,161 kms of North South and East West
Corridors and 486 kms of other highways was approved in December, 2003. Thereafter, works of
preparation of Detailed Project Reports was taken up, which normally takes 12 - 15 months. In
difficult terrain conditions like Jammu and Kashmir and reaches involving wild life, it took even

are under implementation and work for 841 kms is yet to be awarded.
17. After April, 2007 no work under Phase-II could be awarded due to new policy of

remaining projects on BOT (toll) basis.
18. The progress of implementation of Phase-II contracts has been seriously affected due to
problems of land acquisition in the S tates of Assam, West Bengal, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and
Tamil Nadu, delay in permission for tree cutting in U.P. due to insistence of State Government to
provide 10 metres strip of land for afforestation as also serious problem of law and order in
Assam. Progress of some projects is also affected due to slow progress by contractors and
unprecedented increase in prices of cement, steel and bitumen in recent months. Despite these
problems, works already awarded under NHDP Phase-II are likely to be substantially completed by
December, 2009 excepting some major bridges over Brahmaputra, Kosi and Chambal and Agra
bypass and Dholpur town portion, which are contractually scheduled for completion in 2010.
Keeping in view the law and order situation in Assam, some projects are likely to spell over to
2010. The delays are mainly systemic and can be attributed to various reasons and no specific
agency or officer can be said to be responsible.
